```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "Lower trust and compliance barrier to a first sale. Idea A's own brief says buyers expect SOC 2, GDPR/DPA and EU AI Act evidence before adopting a runtime layer in the production path, and a solo six-week build cannot obtain these. Idea B's regulatory needs are a privacy policy and Stripe hosted checkout, scoped as roughly an hour of review plus template drafting.",
    "Simpler buyer for a 90-day first payment. B's payer is an owner-operator contractor who decides alone and pays a monthly card subscription. A's payer is an engineering, platform or security lead placing an unproven one-person vendor inside the execution path where destructive actions happen. A's brief itself calls that 'a high bar.'",
    "Willingness to pay at B's price point is anchored by several sourced live competitors charging without obvious free substitutes: EstimationPro at $66 and $124/mo, Outdoor Estimates at $49.99/mo, QuoteIQ from $29.99/mo. A's field includes a fully free OSS pip package and several generous free tiers, which its brief says 'cap willingness to pay.'",
    "Both fields are crowded: A has nine or more direct competitors, B has seven. A's crowding includes free OSS that directly substitutes for the core feature set, which makes the first conversion harder for a new entrant.",
    "B's brief proposes a concrete narrowing wedge: drop crew scheduling and target a single trade or geography. That makes a minimal paid offering plausible within 90 days. A's differentiation question against JamJet, Retrace and agent-safety-layer stays fully open."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea A's demand evidence shows fear, not purchase intent. The two Reddit quotes express anxiety about agents and describe desirable controls, and the PocketOS incident is a single anecdote. None of the three shows a team paying, or willing to pay, a new third-party vendor rather than adopting free OSS or native framework hooks. A also has a secondary weakness: its main low-cost channel, Show HN, is supported only by a dev-marketing blog's launch guidance, with no conversion data.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-low confidence. B's own evidence is thin. Only one demand quote is sourced; the second has an unretrieved URL and counts as missing. The claim that competitors were built by solo contractor-founders appears without a citation. The $237 cost-per-lead figure is a generic B2B SaaS benchmark, not specific to contractors. A has stronger sourced demand signals. B wins mainly because A's own brief documents structural barriers (compliance, trust in the production path, free OSS substitutes) that bear directly on landing a first paying customer within 90 days."
}
```
